# 1. Project overview

This analysis uses **model-based clustering (`mclust`)** to identify lifestyle
and nutrition subgroups in the cancer-risk dataset.

A key methodological improvement in this version is that **Lifestyle is not
one-hot encoded and fed into a Gaussian mixture model**. `mclust` assumes
continuous variables, so using 0/1 dummy variables as if they were continuous
can artificially inflate distance-based diagnostics such as the Hopkins
statistic.

The clustering model therefore uses only the continuous lifestyle/nutrition
measurements:

- BMI
- Carbohydrates
- Proteins
- Fats
- Vitamin A
- Vitamin C
- Iron

`Lifestyle` is retained for **cluster interpretation**, not as a clustering
input.

# 2. Load packages

```{r libraries}
required_packages <- c(
  "mclust",
  "cluster",
  "ggplot2",
  "tidyr",
  "dplyr",
  "corrplot",
  "factoextra",
  "scales"
)

missing_packages <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop(
    paste0(
      "Missing package(s): ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "),
      ". Install them once with:\ninstall.packages(c(",
      paste0('"', missing_packages, '"', collapse = ", "),
      "))"
    )
  )
}

library(mclust)
library(cluster)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(corrplot)
library(factoextra)
library(scales)
```

# 3. Load the data

The project dataset is a CSV file. The code deliberately checks that the file
exists before trying to read it.

```{r load-data}
data_file <- "crc_data_with_clusters.csv"

if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  stop(
    paste0(
      "Cannot find '", data_file, "'. ",
      "Place the CSV file in the same folder as this Rmd and knit again."
    )
  )
}

df <- read.csv(data_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

cat("Rows:", nrow(df), "\n")
cat("Columns:", ncol(df), "\n")
head(df)
```

## 3.1 Check the structure

```{r structure}
str(df)
```

# 4. Data quality and exploratory analysis

## 4.1 Required columns

```{r required-columns}
required_columns <- c(
  "Participant_ID", "Age", "Gender", "BMI", "Lifestyle",
  "Ethnicity", "Family_History_CRC", "Pre-existing Conditions",
  "Carbohydrates (g)", "Proteins (g)", "Fats (g)",
  "Vitamin A (IU)", "Vitamin C (mg)", "Iron (mg)", "CRC_Risk"
)

missing_required <- setdiff(required_columns, names(df))

if (length(missing_required) > 0) {
  stop(
    paste("The following required columns are missing:",
          paste(missing_required, collapse = ", "))
  )
}

cat("All required columns are present.\n")
```

## 4.2 Remove any old cluster column

The supplied CSV may already contain a `Cluster` column from an earlier run.
It must **not** be used as an input when creating a new clustering solution.

```{r remove-old-cluster}
if ("Cluster" %in% names(df)) {
  df$Cluster <- NULL
  cat("Old Cluster column removed before reclustering.\n")
} else {
  cat("No previous Cluster column found.\n")
}
```

## 4.3 Fix numeric types

```{r numeric-types}
numeric_features <- c(
  "BMI",
  "Carbohydrates (g)",
  "Proteins (g)",
  "Fats (g)",
  "Vitamin A (IU)",
  "Vitamin C (mg)",
  "Iron (mg)"
)

for (v in numeric_features) {
  df[[v]] <- as.numeric(df[[v]])
}

numeric_check <- sapply(df[numeric_features], is.numeric)
print(numeric_check)
```

## 4.4 Missing-value check

```{r missing-values}
missing_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(df),
  Missing = sapply(df, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  Percent = round(
    100 * sapply(df, function(x) sum(is.na(x))) / nrow(df), 2
  )
)

print(missing_summary[order(-missing_summary$Missing), ])
```

For the clustering variables, missing numeric values are replaced by the
**median of that variable**. This keeps the clustering sample size intact and
is less sensitive to extreme values than mean imputation.

```{r impute-clustering}
for (v in numeric_features) {
  if (anyNA(df[[v]])) {
    df[[v]][is.na(df[[v]])] <- median(df[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
  }
}

cat("Missing values in clustering variables after imputation:",
    sum(is.na(df[numeric_features])), "\n")
```

## 4.5 Numeric distributions

```{r distributions}
eda_long <- pivot_longer(
  df[, numeric_features, drop = FALSE],
  cols = everything(),
  names_to = "Feature",
  values_to = "Value"
)

ggplot(eda_long, aes(x = Value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ Feature, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of continuous clustering variables",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Count"
  )
```

## 4.6 Correlation matrix

```{r correlation}
cor_matrix <- cor(df[numeric_features], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

corrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.7,
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  diag = FALSE
)
```

# 5. Prepare the clustering data

## 5.1 Select continuous clustering variables

```{r select-clustering}
cluster_data <- df[, numeric_features, drop = FALSE]

summary(cluster_data)
```

## 5.2 Standardise the variables

Standardisation prevents variables with larger numerical units, especially
Vitamin A, from dominating the model.

```{r scale-data}
cluster_scaled <- scale(cluster_data)

cat("Clustering observations:", nrow(cluster_scaled), "\n")
cat("Clustering variables:", ncol(cluster_scaled), "\n")
```

# 6. Hopkins statistic — clustering tendency

The **Hopkins statistic is a diagnostic**, not proof that clusters exist.

A value around 0.5 is broadly consistent with a random spatial pattern, while
values substantially above 0.5 indicate increasing evidence of non-random
structure. Values extremely close to 1 should be treated cautiously.

Most importantly, this analysis calculates Hopkins **only on continuous
variables**. This avoids the 0/1 dummy-variable problem that can produce an
artificially high value such as 0.998.

```{r hopkins}
set.seed(42)

hopkins_result <- factoextra::get_clust_tendency(
  cluster_scaled,
  n = min(200, nrow(cluster_scaled)),
  graph = FALSE
)

hopkins_value <- hopkins_result$hopkins_stat

cat("Continuous-only Hopkins statistic:",
    round(hopkins_value, 4), "\n")

if (hopkins_value > 0.95) {
  cat(
    "Interpretation: very strong clustering tendency detected. ",
    "This should still be checked against BIC, silhouette and the ",
    "dissimilarity matrix rather than treated as proof of well-separated clusters.\n"
  )
} else if (hopkins_value > 0.75) {
  cat("Interpretation: substantial evidence of non-random structure.\n")
} else if (hopkins_value > 0.60) {
  cat("Interpretation: some evidence of clusterable structure.\n")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: weak evidence of strong cluster structure.\n")
}
```

# 7. Dissimilarity matrix

The full 1,000 × 1,000 matrix is unnecessarily large to display. A random
sample of at most 200 observations is used for a readable and reproducible
heatmap.

The observations are ordered by their eventual cluster assignment so that
possible within-cluster blocks can be seen clearly.

```{r matrix-sample}
set.seed(42)

matrix_n <- min(200, nrow(cluster_scaled))
matrix_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(cluster_scaled)), matrix_n)

matrix_data <- cluster_scaled[matrix_rows, , drop = FALSE]

cat("Observations displayed in dissimilarity matrix:", matrix_n, "\n")
```

The first matrix is shown **before clustering** so that the distance structure
is not visually forced into clusters.

```{r raw-dissimilarity, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
raw_dist <- as.matrix(dist(matrix_data))

image(
  1:nrow(raw_dist),
  1:ncol(raw_dist),
  raw_dist,
  col = hcl.colors(100, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
  axes = FALSE,
  xlab = "Sampled observations",
  ylab = "Sampled observations",
  main = "Dissimilarity matrix — continuous variables"
)

axis(1, at = pretty(seq_len(nrow(raw_dist))))
axis(2, at = pretty(seq_len(nrow(raw_dist))))
box()
```

# 8. Model-based clustering with Mclust

Several possible numbers of clusters are evaluated. BIC is used to select the
best-supported Gaussian mixture model.

```{r mclust}
set.seed(42)

mclust_model <- Mclust(
  cluster_scaled,
  G = 2:8
)

summary(mclust_model)
```

## 8.1 BIC model selection

```{r bic, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
plot(
  mclust_model,
  what = "BIC",
  main = "BIC comparison across candidate cluster solutions"
)
```

```{r optimal-clusters}
optimal_G <- mclust_model$G

cat("BIC-selected number of clusters:", optimal_G, "\n")
cat("Selected covariance model:", mclust_model$modelName, "\n")
```

## 8.2 Attach cluster membership

```{r attach-clusters}
df$Cluster <- factor(mclust_model$classification)

cluster_sizes <- as.data.frame(table(df$Cluster))
names(cluster_sizes) <- c("Cluster", "Count")

print(cluster_sizes)

ggplot(cluster_sizes, aes(x = Cluster, y = Count)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), vjust = -0.3) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of observations in each cluster",
    x = "Cluster",
    y = "Observations"
  )
```

# 9. PCA visualisation

PCA is used only as a **visualisation tool**. The actual clustering model is
still the Mclust model above.

```{r pca}
pca <- prcomp(cluster_scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)

pca_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pca$x[, 1],
  PC2 = pca$x[, 2],
  Cluster = df$Cluster
)

ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, shape = Cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Mclust clusters projected onto the first two principal components",
    x = "Principal Component 1",
    y = "Principal Component 2",
    shape = "Cluster"
  )
```

# 10. Cluster-ordered dissimilarity matrix

Now the same sampled observations are ordered by the Mclust cluster
assignment. Clear diagonal blocks indicate stronger within-cluster similarity;
blurred boundaries indicate overlap.

```{r ordered-matrix, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
sample_clusters <- df$Cluster[matrix_rows]
ordered_index <- order(sample_clusters)

ordered_dist <- raw_dist[ordered_index, ordered_index]

image(
  1:nrow(ordered_dist),
  1:ncol(ordered_dist),
  ordered_dist,
  col = hcl.colors(100, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
  axes = FALSE,
  xlab = "Observations ordered by cluster",
  ylab = "Observations ordered by cluster",
  main = "Dissimilarity matrix — ordered by Mclust cluster"
)

axis(1, at = pretty(seq_len(nrow(ordered_dist))))
axis(2, at = pretty(seq_len(nrow(ordered_dist))))
box()

# Add approximate cluster boundaries.
ordered_labels <- as.character(sample_clusters[ordered_index])
changes <- which(ordered_labels[-1] != ordered_labels[-length(ordered_labels)])
if (length(changes) > 0) {
  abline(v = changes + 0.5, h = changes + 0.5, lty = 2)
}
```

# 11. Cluster quality — silhouette

Silhouette width provides an additional, independent check of separation.

```{r silhouette}
full_dist <- dist(cluster_scaled)

sil <- silhouette(
  as.integer(df$Cluster),
  full_dist
)

average_silhouette <- mean(sil[, "sil_width"])

cat(
  "Average silhouette width:",
  round(average_silhouette, 4),
  "\n"
)

plot(
  sil,
  border = NA,
  main = "Silhouette plot for Mclust cluster assignments"
)
```

```{r silhouette-interpretation}
if (average_silhouette >= 0.50) {
  cat("Interpretation: reasonably strong separation.\n")
} else if (average_silhouette >= 0.25) {
  cat("Interpretation: weak-to-moderate separation; clusters overlap.\n")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: weak separation; cluster assignments should be interpreted cautiously.\n")
}
```

# 12. Cluster profiling

## 12.1 Numeric profile

```{r profile}
profile <- df %>%
  group_by(Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      all_of(numeric_features),
      ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(profile)
```

## 12.2 Standardised cluster fingerprint

```{r profile-fingerprint, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
profile_long <- profile %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Cluster,
    names_to = "Feature",
    values_to = "Mean"
  )

profile_long$Z_Mean <- as.numeric(
  scale(profile_long$Mean)
)

ggplot(
  profile_long,
  aes(x = Feature, y = Z_Mean, fill = Cluster)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Cluster profile fingerprint",
    subtitle = "Standardised cluster means",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Standardised mean",
    fill = "Cluster"
  )
```

## 12.3 Lifestyle composition

Lifestyle was deliberately excluded from the Mclust input. It is now used to
help describe what each cluster looks like.

```{r lifestyle}
lifestyle_table <- table(df$Cluster, df$Lifestyle)
print(lifestyle_table)

lifestyle_df <- as.data.frame(lifestyle_table)
names(lifestyle_df) <- c("Cluster", "Lifestyle", "Count")

ggplot(
  lifestyle_df,
  aes(x = Cluster, y = Count, fill = Lifestyle)
) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Lifestyle composition within each cluster",
    x = "Cluster",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Lifestyle"
  )
```

# 13. Cluster uncertainty

Mclust provides a posterior probability for the assigned cluster. Low
uncertainty means the observation has a clear model-based assignment.

```{r uncertainty}
uncertainty_df <- data.frame(
  Cluster = df$Cluster,
  Uncertainty = mclust_model$uncertainty
)

cat(
  "Mean classification uncertainty:",
  round(mean(uncertainty_df$Uncertainty), 4),
  "\n"
)

ggplot(uncertainty_df, aes(x = Cluster, y = Uncertainty)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Mclust classification uncertainty",
    x = "Cluster",
    y = "Uncertainty"
  )
```

# 14. Overall evaluation summary

```{r evaluation-summary}
cat("========================================\n")
cat("CLUSTERING EVALUATION SUMMARY\n")
cat("========================================\n")
cat("Observations: ", nrow(df), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Variables used by Mclust: ", length(numeric_features), "\n", sep = "")
cat("BIC-selected G: ", optimal_G, "\n", sep = "")
cat("Covariance model: ", mclust_model$modelName, "\n", sep = "")
cat("Continuous-only Hopkins: ", round(hopkins_value, 4), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Average silhouette: ", round(average_silhouette, 4), "\n", sep = "")
cat("Mean uncertainty: ",
    round(mean(mclust_model$uncertainty), 4), "\n", sep = "")
cat("========================================\n")
```

**Important interpretation:** a high Hopkins statistic alone does not establish
that the final clusters are useful. The final judgement should consider
**BIC, silhouette width, the dissimilarity matrix, cluster sizes, uncertainty,
and the substantive cluster profiles together**.

# 15. Save the final clustered dataset

This output is used by the classification analysis.

```{r save-output}
output_file <- "crc_data_with_clusters.csv"

write.csv(
  df,
  output_file,
  row.names = FALSE
)

cat(
  "Saved clustered dataset to:",
  normalizePath(output_file, winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE),
  "\n"
)
```
